newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina sees 6 pct growth in H2, 5-6 pct for 97.
newsitem.headline: Argentina sees 6 pct growth in H2, 5-6 pct for 97.

text.p: Argentina's new Economy Minister Roque Fernandez forecast to business leaders Friday the economy would grow by more than 6.0 percent in the second half of this year and by 5.0-6.0 percent in 1997.

The minister also forecast that Argentina's budget deficit next year would be less than one percent of gross domestic product and "we will return to fiscal balance in 1998." Argentina's GDP totalled about $280 billion last year.

Argentina has overshot fiscal deficit targets this year and Fernandez has warned the shortfall could be $6.6 billion, versus $2.5 billion agreed with the International Monetary Fund, if Congress does not approve his package of fiscal austerity measures submitted as a bill last week.
"All the indicators show we are back to economic growth," he said in a speech to the Argentine Industrial Union. "We have left behind for good the recession produced by 1995's financial crisis."

Last year the Argentine economy shrank 4.4 percent after four years of 7.7 percent average annual growth. But many of the UIA business lobby have criticized Fernandez's package of tax increases as likely to hinder recovery from the Tequila Effect recession.
Fernandez, who replaced Domingo Cavallo a month ago, gave an upbeat economic outlook at a time of political uncertainty and growing pressure for action on unemployment, which stands at 17.1 percent.

"From the first quarter of 1990 to the present day GDP has grown more than 50 percent. This is a unique situation in Argentine history," the former Central Bank chief said. "In the second half of this year we will grow at over six percent and growth for 1997 will be between 5.0-6.0 percent."

Fernandez, an economist trained at the University of Chicago, predicted that an improved relationship between the cost of capital and labor -- a stated aim of his package's reduction in payroll taxes -- would combine with GDP growth "to have a greater positive impact on employment."

He forecast growth in bank loans to $56 billion this year and $65 billion next year, a rise in Central Bank reserves to $22 billion by year-end from their current $18.79 billion, and promised public spending would shrink next year and tax evasion would be reduced.

Fernandez said tax collection was already showing signs of improvement, rising 10 percent in August from the same month last year, and vowed to "reduce taxes as soon as possible, starting with reductions that would improve employment."

Foreign trade grew 5.0 percent in the first half of 1996 while industrial exports and capital goods imports continue firm, said Fernandez, going on to quote recent indicators on labor demand, industrial output and service demand.
